newsitem.title: BRAZIL: BRAZIL DEBT OUTLOOK- Market pins hopes on new cash.
newsitem.headline: BRAZIL DEBT OUTLOOK- Market pins hopes on new cash.

text.p: Brazil debt watchers hope an anticipated slew of fresh money into emerging market funds over the next few weeks will boost underperforming Brazilian Bradys and energize stagnant Eurobond activity.
The Brady market has remained volatile following the Federal Reserve's 25 basis point hike last week, which only fueled fears of additional increases in short term U.S. interest rates.
But players say Brady amortization and interest payments in April totaling some $4.0 billion - -with about half of that coming from Brazil -- should send buyers back to the market.
The Brady market should also see support from second-quarter portfolio reshuffling and the end of the Japanese fiscal year, which was expected to boost U.S. Treasury demand.
Traders say underperforming Brazilian Bradys stand the most to gain in a market rally.

"People have been buying things like Panama and Ecuador and selling Brazilian C bonds to hedge. This is one reason we think Brazil is undervalued, so when the market rallies, Brazil will be one of the biggest winners," said Pedro Barbosa, chief of Brady debt trading in Brazil for ING Bank.
Still, fixed rate Cs remain tied to the U.S. Treasury market and U.S. economic data, which means they could face a bumpy ride in coming weeks, traders said.
Brady switches to consider include a move into floating rate Brazilian NMBs and out of DCBS.
NMBs are now trading at about 420 bp over U.S. Treasuries, or only 30 bp tighter than DCBS. The target range for the spread between the two instruments is 60 bp, traders said.
Also, many Brazilian and some U.S. accounts are believed to be long on DCBs, meaning any activity in the market could see a selloff of DCBs and thereby help NMBs.

Traders said another option was a move into Venezuelan DCBS and out of Brazilian EIs. For the past six months, Venezuelan DCBS have generally traded about 10 bp to 15 bp wider than EIs. Partly due to technical reasons, that spread has widened to about 100 bp.
Players suggest switching back when the spread narrows to about 35 bp.
Upcoming Brazilian Eurobond deals have not generated too much enthusiasm, and players hope a revitalized Brady market may pull Eurobond buyers from the sidelines.

Banco do Brasil's $400 million 10-year deal via UBS was expected to price sometime over the next few weeks at about 265 bp over Treasuries, considered on the pricey side. Traders said the issue would draw a lot more attention at 280-300 bp over.

Cesp's upcoming $200 million 10-year, put-able at five, looked even less appealing after the company's release last week of a whopping 513 million reais ($484 million) 1996 loss, on top of a 193.6 million real loss the year before.
"The last Cesp deal ZSED had a sovereign guarantee and this is not coming with that appeal," added one trader.
Secondary Eurobond trade has been subdued by the long Easter holiday, which closed New York on Friday and London today.
Traders spotted few good deals in well-known Brazilian paper, suggesting a look at longer-dated, higher risk debt.
Players saw a lot of room for tightening in Tevecap's 12-5/8 percent due 2004 ZRIT. The eight-year issue closed Friday at 495 bp over U.S. Treasuries, after widening about 15 bp over the week.

Telecom's eight-year 10-3/4 percent due 2004 ZUWD widened about 15 bp on the week, closing at 305 bp over Treasuries. The paper is especially attractive because it carries a guarantee from federally owned Telebras.

Banco Bamerindus debt holders were happy following last week's announcement that HSBC Holdings Plc had taken over the troubled bank and assumed its liabilities. Bamerindus paper is not liquid, however, and the news had little to no effect on Brazilian bank debt, traders said.
((--Sao Paulo newsroom, 5511 248-5414))
